newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Air carriers slow to embrace container pool.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Air carriers slow to embrace container pool.

text.p: If the world's airlines were to pool their 520,000 cargo containers, the industry could save over $160 million annually and improve service to customers, industry experts told a cargo conference here.
Yet promoters say their proposal for a global container pool is battling inertia and skepticism from the carriers.
A project team from Transamerica Leasing Inc briefed the International Air Transport Association's IATA Cargo Week 97 delegates on its proposal to set up and manage a global container pool.
The company is a leading transportation leasing concern which provides marine containers, trucks, rail cars and even truck axles.

Airlines now own or lease their own containers. Out of fear of being left short, they tend to have more than they need, about seven container sets per widebody aircraft, said Brian Tracey, a senior Transamerica vice president.
A pool might maintain as few as 3.5 sets per aircraft and carriers still would be better supplied than they are today.

Transamerica would establish depots and repair facilities worldwide, as well as a centralized management and control system for what are also known to airlines and their cargo customers as Unit Load Devices, or ULDs.

The pool would handle repositioning of equipment and use massive buying power to lower the cost of new containers. It would gradually bring more standardization to the world's container fleet, and invest in developing lighter weight ULDs. Airlines would have fewer equipment shortages.

A standard full size container for a widebody aircraft costs $1,000-$1,100. Maintaining a full complement for a widebody aircraft - typically 56 boxes - can cost upward of $250,000 in capital and operating costs a year, including the cost of repairs. Carriers end up ferrying around empty containers to position them where needed, an added expense.
Switching from the current system to a pooling arrangement based on variable costs (fee per usage) would save the industry more than $160 million a year, said Transamerica.

Yet, the reaction of one senior cargo executive at Cargo Week 97 summarized the mood towards the Transamerica proposal: "It doesn't give me a warm and fuzzy feeling," he told Reuters. His airline, he said, doesn't have a ULD problem. It has a large ULD fleet and makes a tidy sum from demurrage - the per-diem fees paid by other carriers to use its containers as they move around the world.

Other airlines fear a pool would mean loss of control over container availability - possibly leading to shortages in peak periods, and lost business. Still others insist they have high standards in ULDs, and that pooling would mean using another airline's substandard equipment.
The total scheduled airline container fleet represents a capital investment of over $1 billion. By 2002, that will almost double.
ULDs are inexpensive assets compared to overall assets, but an industry that spends up to $500 million annually managing $1 billion in assets could be ready for a change," says Tracey.
The idea to develop an industry ULD pool originated with a group of airlines, predominantly from North America. They approached companies like Transamerica to generate a proposal.

Now, the industry is slow to embrace the concept, partly, said Tracey, because they have so many more pressing concerns "It doesn't seem to get the attention within the airlines that you would think."

By end 1997, it should be clear whether Transamerica's idea will be accepted. By By June, it will unveil a full operational model, including details of how the depots would be set up, how equipment tracking will work, how carriers would be billed and how the project would be phased in.

After Transamerica shows its model to the carriers, someone will have to step forward and sign up in the months that follow, said Tracey. Otherwise, Transamerica may have to throw in the towel and look at other ways of entering the airline container field, he added.
